title: You’re Afraid of Dying—but Maybe What Terrifies You Most Is Finally Losing Control
paragraphs: You’re Afraid of Dying—but Maybe What Terrifies You Most Is Finally Losing Control

You can control the appointment. The medication. The retirement account. The locks on the door. The food you eat. The people you call. But eventually every human being reaches a door that cannot be negotiated with—and Hebrews says Jesus Christ walked through that door first so fear would no longer have to own you.
There is a thought most of us know how to push away.
Until 2:13 in the morning.
Until the doctor says, “We found something.”
Until someone your age dies.
Until you stand beside a hospital bed watching a chest rise... fall... rise... fall...
Until you attend the funeral of someone who was laughing in photographs only weeks before.
Until your parents begin looking older.
Until your children start asking questions about what happens when people die.
Until you notice that the face in the mirror is changing too.
Then suddenly the thought you have spent years keeping outside gets through the door.
One day, I am going to die.
And perhaps what makes that sentence so terrifying is not merely death itself.
Perhaps it is the unbearable realization that, when that moment comes, you will finally encounter something you cannot control.
We spend enormous portions of our lives trying to manage uncertainty.
Calendars.
Insurance.
Savings.
Checkups.
Security systems.
Passwords.
Backup plans.
Five-year plans.

We monitor our bodies. We make plans for tomorrow. We worry about our children. We try to protect what we love. None of those things are inherently wrong. Scripture does not condemn wisdom, stewardship, preparation, or legitimate care for life.
But underneath good preparation can sometimes hide another hunger.
If I can control enough, perhaps nothing can truly hurt me.
Then death whispers the sentence human pride hates hearing:
You are not God.
You cannot negotiate another century into your lungs.
You cannot command your heart to beat forever.
You cannot accumulate enough money to purchase immortality.

You cannot become successful enough, attractive enough, careful enough, powerful enough, religious enough, or admired enough to make your body exempt from the sentence that has followed humanity since Eden.
And this is precisely where Christianity refuses to offer us sentimental comfort.
The Gospel does not tell us death is imaginary.
It tells us death has been confronted.
Hebrews 2:14–15 says of Jesus:

“Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.”
Listen closely to the language.
The New Testament was written here in Greek, and the words are startling:
“ἵνα διὰ τοῦ θανάτου καταργήσῃ... καὶ ἀπαλλάξῃ τούτους... φόβῳ θανάτου... δουλείας.”
At the heart of the passage are words about death, liberation, fear, and slavery.
Thanatos — θάνατος — death.
Phobos — φόβος — fear.
Douleia — δουλεία — slavery or bondage.
And then there is that powerful verb associated with what Christ accomplished: katargeō — καταργέω.
Translations sometimes render the thought with “destroy,” while others communicate the sense as breaking or nullifying the enemy’s power.
That distinction matters.
Hebrews is not saying Satan ceased to exist at Calvary. Scripture clearly continues to speak about spiritual opposition after the cross.
It is saying something more precise and glorious.

Through His own death, Jesus broke the tyrannical claim of the one who wielded death as an instrument of terror, and He came to liberate people who had spent their lives enslaved by the fear of dying.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not shame you for recognizing mortality.
It does not say a Christian can never tremble in a hospital room.
It does not say believers never grieve.
It does not tell you that faith means pretending death is pleasant.
Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus’s tomb.
Christian courage is not emotional numbness.
Christian hope is not pretending the grave does not hurt.
The miracle is deeper.
You can be frightened without belonging to fear.
You can weep without surrendering to despair.
You can face mortality without mortality becoming your master.
Because Christianity ultimately does not give you an argument against death.
It gives you a Person who entered death...
and came out alive.
That changes everything.
Jesus did not save humanity while remaining safely distant from humanity.
Hebrews says He shared our “flesh and blood.”
Think about that.
The eternal Son entered the vulnerability we desperately spend our lives trying to escape.
He knew hunger.
Weariness.
Pain.
Rejection.
Blood.
Tears.
And death.
The hands through which creation came were eventually pierced by nails.
The lungs that breathed earthly air stopped breathing.
The heart inside the incarnate Son stopped beating.
His body was placed inside a tomb.
Christianity does not proclaim a God who watched human suffering from a protected balcony in heaven.
It proclaims Jesus Christ crucified.
And then it proclaims the empty tomb.
This is why the Gospel can look death directly in the face without pretending death is harmless.
Death is an enemy.
But it is a defeated enemy.
Paul erupts in 1 Corinthians 15 with almost defiant joy:
“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
Not because Christians never die.
They do.
Not because funerals stop hurting.
They do not.
Not because separation becomes painless.
It does not.
But because Christ has risen, physical death no longer gets the final sentence over those who belong to Him.
And maybe this is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
What exactly are you afraid of losing?
Your body?
Your family?
Your plans?
Your possessions?
Your unfinished dreams?
Your independence?
Your reputation?
Your ability to decide what happens next?
Maybe you say you fear death.
But beneath that fear may be another confession:
I am terrified of surrender.
Because surrender means acknowledging that your life was never ultimately yours to control.
You received it.
Every heartbeat has been mercy.
Every sunrise has been borrowed.
Every person you love is a gift rather than a possession.
Every breath enters your lungs because God permits another moment.
That realization can feel frightening until you understand whose hands are holding the life you cannot hold forever.
Jesus does not ask you to surrender your life into emptiness.
He asks you to entrust yourself to Him.
There is an enormous difference.
Christian surrender is not falling blindly into darkness.
It is placing yourself into the hands that were pierced for you.
Maybe you have spent decades calling yourself a Christian while quietly constructing your entire existence around avoiding vulnerability.
Maybe you pray, but only after your plans fail.
Maybe you trust God—as long as God follows your schedule.
Maybe you say, “Your will be done,” while internally adding, “provided Your will looks reasonably similar to mine.”
And mortality exposes the arrangement.
Death tears the contract in half.
Suddenly the illusion disappears.
You were never sovereign.
Neither was I.
And strangely...
that can become the beginning of freedom.
Because if you were responsible for keeping yourself alive forever, you would have every reason to panic.
If your eternity depended upon maintaining perfect control, you would have every reason to despair.
If salvation depended upon your ability to become righteous enough before your heart stops beating, none of us could sleep tonight.
But that is not the Gospel.
The Gospel is not:
Control yourself well enough and perhaps you can save yourself.
The Gospel is:
Christ came for sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
Christ forgives.
Christ reconciles.
Christ saves.
Christ holds His people.
Jesus said in John 11:25:
“I am the resurrection, and the life.”
Notice what He did not say.
“I know an interesting philosophy concerning resurrection.”
“I can teach you coping mechanisms for mortality.”
“I possess information about eternal life.”
No.
“I am.”
Christian hope ultimately rests not in our ability to understand every mystery surrounding death but in Jesus Christ Himself.
That means the deepest answer to the fear of dying is not gaining more control.
It is discovering Someone trustworthy enough that you can finally release control.
Maybe you are reading this while healthy.
Then do not waste the mercy of today.
Maybe you are reading this after receiving frightening medical news.

Then hear this without cheap promises: Christianity does not guarantee that every illness will disappear in this life. But Jesus Christ promises something immeasurably greater than pretending mortality does not exist.
He offers Himself.
Maybe you are old enough that death no longer feels theoretical.
Your friends' names have begun appearing in funeral announcements.
Rooms once filled with familiar voices are quieter now.
Your body reminds you that time is moving.
You sometimes wonder how many Christmas mornings remain.
How many birthdays.
How many ordinary breakfasts.
How many times you will hug the people you love.
There is tenderness in that fear.
But there can also be hope.
Your aging body is not evidence that Jesus has forgotten you.
And if you belong to Christ, the approaching end of earthly life is not the approaching end of your story.
Maybe you are twenty-two and death terrifies you precisely because you have barely begun living.
You want marriage.
Children.
Travel.
Achievement.
A home.
A career.
You have places you still want to see and things you desperately want to become.
You cannot imagine leaving now.
That desire to live is not something you need to be ashamed of.
Life is a gift.
But do not make the gift your god.
Because anything you demand must last forever before you can have peace will eventually become your master.
Only Christ can bear the weight of your eternity.
And maybe your fear is even deeper than dying.
Maybe you fear meeting God.
Because beneath all the religious language, you know things about yourself nobody else knows.
The secret.
The betrayal.
The pornography.
The affair.
The lie.
The bitterness.
The years of pretending.
The abortion you never talk about.
The person you never forgave.
The person from whom you desperately need forgiveness.
The double life.
The hidden addiction.
The private arrogance.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The God you have spent years avoiding.
Death frightens you because eternity makes secrecy feel temporary.
If that is you, please understand something before shame convinces you to run farther away.
The answer is not pretending your sin is smaller.
The answer is discovering that Christ is greater.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity needed minor improvement.
He went because sinners needed reconciliation with a holy God.
The scandal of the cross is that the innocent Christ suffered for the guilty.
And the grace of the Gospel is that guilty people who could never rewrite their own past can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and given new life through Him.
This is where our message becomes more than a slogan.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin as virtue.
Not by telling us judgment does not matter.
Grace is costly precisely because sin is real.
At Calvary, Christ did not sweep evil underneath the universe's carpet.
He bore sin.
The cross reveals simultaneously how serious our rebellion is and how astonishing God's mercy is.
And resurrection announces that death did not win.
So what if tonight, instead of asking God for another illusion of control, you finally gave Him the thing you have been desperately protecting?
Yourself.
Not your polished religious version.
Not your Sunday version.
Not the Facebook version.
You.
The frightened you.
The guilty you.
The aging you.
The anxious you.
The person who sometimes wakes in darkness wondering what happens when the heart finally stops.
Bring that person to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop trying to negotiate your own resurrection.
You cannot save yourself.
That is not an insult.
That is the doorway to grace.
Because the moment you stop demanding to be your own savior, you can finally look toward the Savior who already entered the grave for sinners.
And He did not remain there.
The resurrection of Jesus is why Christian hope is radically different from positive thinking.
Positive thinking says, “Hopefully everything works out.”
The Gospel announces that Christ is risen.
Positive thinking tells you to suppress the frightening thought.
The Gospel allows you to stare at the grave and still confess that Jesus is Lord.
Positive thinking depends upon your emotional state.
Christian hope depends upon Christ.
You may have trembling hands and genuine faith at the same time.
You may need someone beside your hospital bed and still belong completely to Jesus.
You may cry when you think about leaving your children and still believe in resurrection.
Faith is not always loud.
Sometimes faith sounds like a frightened person whispering through tears:
“Jesus... I trust You.”
And perhaps those are the words somebody reading this needs tonight.
Not, “I understand everything.”
Not, “I am no longer human.”
Not, “Nothing scares me.”
Just:
“Jesus... I trust You.”
Let another believer see your name and pray.
Someone younger than you may desperately need to hear that faith can survive the night they are currently facing.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page either.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
Your mother.
Your father.
Your former classmate fighting cancer.
The twenty-year-old having panic attacks.
The believer who has attended church for forty years but still trembles when thinking about the grave.
The unbelieving friend who has never seriously considered eternity.
Fear has a way of returning at inconvenient hours, and you may need these Scriptures again when the room becomes quiet and your mind becomes loud.
It cannot.
Not because God needs your money.
He does not.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
Because somebody you know is going to die.
So are you.
So am I.
That sentence does not have to be cruel.
It can become an invitation.
An invitation to stop postponing repentance.
To stop rationing forgiveness.
To stop treating tomorrow as property you already own.
To say “I love you” while there is still breath.
To reconcile where reconciliation is possible.
To confess what needs confessing.
To forgive.
To live awake.
To stop worshiping control.
To stop hiding from God.
And to entrust your life and your death to Jesus Christ.
One day your calendar will contain appointments you will never attend.
Your phone will contain messages you will never answer.
Your closet will contain clothes somebody else will eventually move.
The world will continue turning without asking your permission.
That sounds terrifying...
until you remember that the universe was never resting on your shoulders.
It rests beneath the authority of Christ.
You were never asked to defeat death.
Jesus already entered that battle.
You were never asked to resurrect yourself.
You were called to trust the risen Christ.

Hebrews speaks directly into the prison humanity has built around mortality: Christ shared our flesh and blood, entered death, broke the tyrannical hold associated with death, and came to liberate those enslaved by its fear.
So perhaps freedom does not begin when you finally discover how to control death.
Perhaps freedom begins when death can no longer control how you live.
And maybe tonight, for the first time, you can loosen your grip.
Not because the grave disappeared.
Because Jesus walked out of one.
Because one day you will finally lose control of everything you spent your lifetime trying to hold.
But if you are in Christ, you will not lose Him.
